newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 16.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 16.

text.p: Prime Minister Jim Bolger used his first MMP coalition cabinet to move rising stars up National's ranks, dump non-performing ministers and placate potential rebels. The NZ First leader, Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters -- who was not present at the announcement -- said NZ First's presence in the Cabinet gave Maori, youth and women greater representation in decision making. Peters said NZ First's cabinet ministers were the four party MPs who had been in parliament before the election and John Delamere, who has been made associate treasurer. Finance minister Bill Birch, who is junior to Peters,

does not have a deputy. Bolger brushed aside suggestions that National would be dominated in the economic area. The new cabinet will be sworn in on Monday, with its first full working session on Wednesday. Page 1.

Sunday's cabinet announcement ended the United NZ Party's coalition with National, with sole party MP Peter Dunne saying he would no longer provide guaranteed support. This effectively reduces the coalition's majority to two votes. Dunne lost his cabinet job and the revenue and internal affairs portfolios. Dunne said he was bitterly disappointed but not surprised.

Others to be demoted were former conservation minister Denis Marshall, former social welfare minister Peter Gresham and two former ministers outside the Cabinet, Roger Maxwell and Katherine O'Regan. Page 1.

Labour leader Helen Clark is unhappy that the Alliance has leaked notes from a confidential briefing on Labour's coalition stance. The Alliance gave reporters a six-page paper on Sunday detailing Labour's coalition offer to NZ First. Clark said no papers had been given to the Alliance by Labour because the briefing had been done by overhead projector and the paper was
purely the Alliance's work. She said the paper "completely misunderstood" some of Labour's positions. Page 2.

Reconstituted tomato processor Cedenco Foods expects to return to profitability in the 1997 financial year after reporting a previously forecast net loss of NZ$6.1 million in the year ended September 30. The company, which recently transferred its tomato business from Gisborne to Australia, said its net operating loss after tax came to $1.4 million, with one-off restructuring costs and writedowns associated with the establishment of Cedenco Australia and the restructuring of the

remaining domestic food business confirmed at a further $4.7 million. "Cedenco expects a return to profitability from its restructured New Zealand operations and the impact of earnings from Cedenco Australia," said managing director Dean Witters. Page 17.

The loss of 120 jobs announced on Friday should enable Fletcher Challenge to integrate its forestry operations with those of Forestry Corporation within a year, the company said. Fletcher Challenge is the operating partner within a consortium that bought the corporation from the government in August for

$2.03 billion. Fletcher Forests spokeswoman Ginny Radford said full integration of the businesses might take up to three years, but operations should be brought together within the year. In August, the company said it expected to save at least $18 million annualy from operating the combined 300,000-hectare forestry estate in the central North Island. Page 17.

A 0.6 percent rise in manufacturing sales in the September quarter was the lowest quarterly rise since September 1991, deputy government statistician Ian Ewing said. Total sales were worth $11.9 billion in the quarter compared with $11.8 billion
for the corresponding quarter last year, but sectors were mixed. Page 17.

Her new ministerial position, Youth Affairs, is one of the least demanding portfolios, and more of her energy is likely to be spent in her associates' jobs: helping Jenny Shipley with accident compensation and Simon Upton with environment.

Support for NZ First has slumped in a poll taken just after the party decided to go into coalition with National. More than a third of those who voted for NZ First at the election have bolted, mainly, it appears, to Labour which is now the most

popular party. The poll commissioned by the New Zealand Herald also found that if another referendum on MMP had been held last week, most people would have voted against it. NZ First, which won 13.4 percent of the party vote at the election, received just 8.2 percent in the survey. Its loss bears comparison to the 46 percent of NZ First voters sampled who said they were not happy with the party's choice of coalition partner. The latest party standings are Labour, 35 percent, National 34 percent, the Alliance 9.2 percent, NZ First 8.2 percent, Act NZ 6.4 percent.

Some of New Zealand Stock Exchange sectoral indices contain very few stocks. Because of this the indices themselves can seem a bit suspect in terms of having much to say about the overall share price trend of a group of companies brought together on the basis of sharing common business activities. However, at the moment there are promising things happening in three such small sectorial areas -- building, engineering, and chemicals and fertilisers. All the stocks in these areas are performing strongly. Three are now trading around their February 1994 highs, achieved just before the United States Federal Reserve hiked interest rates. To be back to early 1994 prices is a
strong showing for shares in a market still struggling to reach those earlier levels on index measures.
